author: chinesechessoutloud
title: Pikafish 2026-09-06 is now on LiXiangQi
intro: From the early PC programs to engines that challenged champions: a short history of computer xiangqi, where Pikafish stands today, and how to study with it on LiXiangQi.

image.alt: Black ink fish within a vermilion brush circle, beside a red horse token, on ivory paper. Pikafish 2026-09-06.

markdown:
LiXiangQi has upgraded its analysis engine to Pikafish 2026-09-06. If you have used the analysis board to check a sacrifice or look for a better defense, Pikafish is the program calculating those continuations. The upgrade brings a newer engine and its trained neural network to your browser.


Having a strong opponent available whenever you want to study is something xiangqi players have been working toward for decades. The early programs were beatable, sometimes entertainingly so. Eventually, even champions had something to learn from them.


## From early PCs to the master's table

One of the first major names was *Xiangqi Master* (象棋大師). Computer-xiangqi researcher Hsu Shun-chin (許舜欽) identifies it as the winner of Taiwan's first computer-xiangqi competition in 1987. Research had begun earlier: his account traces local work to around 1981, when programs could manage only simple endgames. Playing a complete game on a personal computer was itself an achievement. [Hsu's historical account, reproduced on National Taiwan University's xiangqi forum](https://www.ptt.cc/bbs/NTUCHESS/M.1235372762.A.EA3.html), gives a useful picture of that gradual progress.


For home players, an early success was Yu Xishun's (虞希舜) *Jiangzu* (将族), released in 1991. A [Chinese study of xiangqi software](https://www.wxf-xiangqi.org/images/hangzhou-chess/201902_38.pdf) describes its appeal as a game as well as an engine. In a [2005 interview with the developers of Xiangqi Shijia (象棋世家)](https://dpxq.com/magzine/14_qryd_1.htm), Oldwu remembered playing Jiangzu around 1993, sometimes all night, against characters including the Monkey King and Zhu Bajie. He also remembered how far it still seemed from the strongest humans. It offered an opponent at home, with personalities to work through and reasons to keep playing.


During the 1990s and early 2000s, better calculation, position evaluation, opening books, and endgame knowledge made the programs harder to beat. Hsu records that National Taiwan University's ELP reached five-dan status in human competition in 1998 and six-dan in 2001. Meanwhile, the Shijia developers described tools for replaying games, setting up positions, and trying a player's own move before letting the engine continue. The familiar process of testing an idea on an analysis board was already taking shape.


In August 2006, a team of programs including Qitian Dasheng (棋天大圣), Xiangqi Qibing (象棋奇兵), and Xiangqi Cyclone (象棋旋风) narrowly beat five Chinese masters, 11–9. Hsu's account records the individual results. Days later, Xu Yinchuan (许银川) faced the Langchao Tiansuo computer system and [drew both games](https://sports.sina.com.cn/go/2006-08-15/15562398096.shtml).


Xu's [interview afterward](https://sports.sina.com.cn/go/2006-08-15/19582398401.shtml) is more revealing than the score. He described a defender that felt no psychological pressure and could find counterplay from a worse position. A quiet cannon move surprised him. He said he had learned from the games, but also missed facing a person whose expressions he could read. A promising attack now had to survive an opponent that would keep calculating instead of becoming discouraged.


## How engines changed studying

By the late 2010s, programs such as Mingshou (象棋名手), Cyclone, and AlphaCat were established choices for serious analysis. The Chinese software study describes both professionals and enthusiasts buying engines to examine positions, along with the cost of licenses and powerful computers. A [2019 paper by Hu Guiping (胡贵平)](https://www.wxf-xiangqi.org/images/hangzhou-chess/0105_5___2019.pdf) describes software helping players investigate openings, middlegames, and endgames, and judges the leading programs stronger than even top human players.


For studying, the useful change was the ability to challenge an annotation. A book might recommend an attack; an engine could help you investigate the defense it left out. You could return to the position where your own game went wrong and test the move you had considered but rejected. The earlier Shijia interview already describes that kind of interaction: the player supplies an idea, and the computer works through what follows.


Neural networks brought another change. Older engines relied heavily on evaluation rules written by programmers. Pikafish uses NNUE, a neural network trained to evaluate positions, together with a search that calculates possible continuations. Its design reuses much of the previous calculation when a piece moves, making it practical on a normal computer processor. The [Pikafish team's Chinese explanation of NNUE](https://www.pikafish.com/wiki/faq/nnue.html) describes how the two work together. The network helps judge a position; the search still has to investigate the moves.


## Where Pikafish fits

Pikafish (皮卡鱼) appeared in August 2022. Its creator, PikaCat, tells the story in a [Chinese account of the project's beginnings](https://www.bilibili.com/opus/765167201612201986): as a child, he wondered how the Mingshou engine could play xiangqi. Years later, after writing an engine of his own and experimenting with neural networks, he adapted the chess engine Stockfish to xiangqi. He recalls spending three weeks on that conversion. The name combines his earlier “PikaCat” identity with Stockfish, known in Chinese as 鳕鱼.


Today, Pikafish belongs among the leading xiangqi engines. In [tester Kaka's October 9, 2026 comparison](https://bbs.pikafish.org/forum.php?extra=&mod=viewthread&tid=179), Pikafish 2026-09-25 ranks first among the tested versions, ahead of Cyclone NN and Xiaochong NN. That is a result from a particular test using deliberately unbalanced starting positions, not an official world title. These engine ratings also belong to their own test pool; they are not human tournament ratings.


Its availability is especially useful to players. The [Chinese Pikafish website](https://www.pikafish.com/) offers downloads, a browser version, and study guidance. The engine's code is open, and the project offers free noncommercial use; its neural-network files have separate terms. Strong analysis is accessible without buying a commercial engine.


LiXiangQi currently runs *2026-09-06*. The Chinese project website and its [September release announcement](https://bbs.pikafish.org/forum.php?extra=&mod=viewthread&tid=271) also offer *2026-09-25*. The version used in the ranking above is therefore newer than the version running on LiXiangQi.


## Try the move you didn't play

On LiXiangQi, ordinary xiangqi analysis runs on your own device, using Pikafish's full network. The first use needs a substantial download, which the browser can retain for later sessions. The time it takes to analyze a position depends on your device and how long you let it search.


Open the [analysis board](https://lixiangqi.com/analysis), choose Xiangqi, and enable local evaluation. Bring up a completed game and stop before a difficult decision. First, work out your own candidate move and the reply you expect. Then play your idea on the board and inspect the engine's continuation.


If a cannon sacrifice fails, look for the defense that makes it fail. If the engine prefers a quiet move, follow the line until you can see what it improves. Return to the original position and try your opponent's most stubborn reply. An evaluation number tells you which side the engine prefers; working through the moves helps you understand why.
